name: The AI Enablement Audit in Investment Firms
title: The AI Enablement Audit in Investment Firms
answer: The AI enablement audit in investment firms examines how artificial intelligence is used across investment processes, from research and portfolio construction to trading, compliance, and client reporting. It maps where models, data feeds, and automated decision systems sit within the firm's workflows and identifies which functions rely on them. The audit also distinguishes between tools that support human judgment and systems that make or execute decisions with limited human review. It covers both internally developed models and third-party AI services, including large language models and predictive analytics. The goal is to produce an inventory of AI dependencies that a fiduciary can review.

sections.body: The AI enablement audit in investment firms examines how artificial intelligence is used across investment processes, from research and portfolio construction to trading, compliance, and client reporting. It maps where models, data feeds, and automated decision systems sit within the firm's workflows and identifies which functions rely on them. The audit also distinguishes between tools that support human judgment and systems that make or execute decisions with limited human review. It covers both internally developed models and third-party AI services, including large language models and predictive analytics. The goal is to produce an inventory of AI dependencies that a fiduciary can review.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The audit looks at the technical substrate on which AI runs, including where models are trained or fine-tuned, where inference happens, and how data flows from market data vendors and internal systems into AI tools. It documents compute resources, model registries, version control, and logging arrangements. The review also checks whether the firm uses external model providers through application programming interfaces or hosts open-weight models on its own infrastructure. It records the operational environment, including failover procedures and monitoring for outages or degraded performance.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is typically done through a structured review that combines questionnaires, interviews with portfolio managers, quants, compliance staff, and information technology teams, and examination of model cards, validation reports, and change logs. Auditors sample model outputs against benchmarks and test for data quality, feature drift, and performance decay. They apply control frameworks adapted from model risk management practice, such as principles similar to those in supervisory guidance on model risk, without treating them as legal requirements. Each AI use case is assigned a risk rating and documented findings that describe how the system behaves in practice.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: This part of the audit traces the provenance of training data and model weights, checks for restricted or improperly licensed data, and reviews contracts with AI vendors for rights to use outputs and data. It examines who can approve model changes, who is accountable when a model errs, and how the firm records that accountability. The audit also looks at bias, explainability, and privacy risks that could affect clients or fiduciaries. It assesses whether AI use conflicts with fiduciary duty, such as systems that steer clients toward products that benefit the firm more than the client.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The AI enablement audit is moving from periodic, manual reviews toward continuous monitoring of AI systems, with audit logs linked to model performance dashboards and automated drift alerts. As regulators publish more guidance on AI in financial services, the audit is likely to become a standard part of annual compliance and fiduciary reviews. Its scope may expand to include generative AI used in client communications and internal research, and to track the provenance of synthetic data used for testing. Firms are also beginning to treat the audit as a living record that updates when new models or data sources are introduced.
